newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: UN STARTS TO REMOVE ARMS FROM IRAQ FOR EXAMINATION.
newsitem.headline: UN STARTS TO REMOVE ARMS FROM IRAQ FOR EXAMINATION.

text.p: United Nations experts have started packing scrapped missile engine parts from Iraq to fly them to the United States through Bahrain, U.N. arms envoy Rolf Ekeus said on Sunday.
Earlier in the day Iraq said it agreed to let the United Nations take scrapped missile engines out of the country for examination.

"We have started (the process)...today. But the process will take a little time. Some of the items have been packed," Ekeus told reporters after arriving in Manama, field headquarters of U.N. missions visiting Iraq under 1991 Gulf War ceasefire terms.
The United Nations wants to establish if scrapped parts are from missing Soviet-made engines as Iraq maintains or are local equipment buried to divert attention from hidden missile engines.

Asked where these parts will be tested, Ekeus said: "It is not definitely decided yet. We will send these items to the United States of America. There, we will have international experts to give us advise. Some items then will stay."
Iraq had objected to the nearly 100 scrapped engines and parts being analysed in the United States although it said it would allow inspection in Russia or France.

"The government of Iraq agreed to the removal of remnants of proscribed missile engines from Iraq for in-depth analysis by the U.N. Special Commission on Iraq (UNSCOM)," Ekeus told a news conference in Baghdad on Sunday with Iraqi Foreign Ministry Undersecretary Riyad al-Qeisi.

Ekeus arrived in Baghdad on Thursday and held extensive meetings with Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz during a four-day visit that ended with a joint statement outlining future cooperation. He said the shipping of the parts was "the hottest issue" in his talks in Baghdad.
The analysis will be carried out with the assistance of a team of international experts, under the supervision of the UNSCOM at laboratories offered by contributing governments.

"It was agreed that the commission will communicate to the government of Iraq the findings of the analysis as they become available and that the commission's conclusions thereon, will not be reported or made public without consultations with the government of Iraq," the joint statement said.
The statement, made available to reporters in Bahrain, was signed by Aziz and Ekeus.
Ekeus said the United States had offered to transport parts of missiles. They will be flown to Bahrain from Baghdad en route to the United States.
The components were unearthed in excavations last year. Iraq said it destroyed the missiles in 1992 and Ekeus said unilateral scrapping of banned items by Iraq had complicated his work.
He said Iraq claimed to have unilaterally dismantled a large portion of its long-range missiles and production tools.
"This you can imagine creates a lot of deep concern," he said.

Ekeus did not say how many missiles he believed were missing but said Iraq could still be concealing equipment. Under terms of the 1991 Gulf War that drove Iraq from Kuwait, Baghdad cannot have missiles with ranges greater than 150 km (93 miles).
Ekeus said his commission still had "quite substantial and serious" concerns about Iraq's chemical arms, which are also banned.
The joint statement said Ekeus would visit Baghdad in the first week of April, before his formal report to the United Nations on April 11.
Ekeus must certify Iraq has no weapons of mass destruction before the United Nations will lift curbs on Iraqi oil exports, although Baghdad is allowed limited oil exports under a humanitarian deal.
